title: Dominican Republic, Serving the US, Expels Cuban Diplomats, Yet Ties with Cuba Have Their Appeal
author: Tom Whitney
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Dominican_Republic_flag_at_the_Hispanic_Day_Parade-680x481.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/26/dominican-
republic-serving-the-us-expels-cuban-diplomats-yet-ties-with-cuba-have-their-
appeal/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Dominican_Republic_flag_at_the_Hispanic_Day_Parade-680x481.jpg)

Photograph Source: Paul Stein from New Jersey, USA - [CC BY-SA
2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/)

The Dominican Republic expelled nine Cuban diplomats on April 13; Cuba claimed
[10](https://barrigaverde.net/preguntas-que-no-responde-un-vasallo-del-siglo-
xxi-llamado-luis-abinader/) . The day marked the centennial of Fidel Castro’s
birth. A celebratory three-hour “political-cultural gala” was taking place at
the Autonomous University of Santo Domingo. News of the action spread.
Attendance at the event swelled to [over
2000](http://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2026/08/14/dirigentes-politicos-de-la-
oposicion-dominicana-denuncia-que-expulsion-de-diplomaticos-cubanos-responde-
a-presiones-de-ee-uu-video/).

Journalist Pablo McKinney wrote that, “I’ve never felt so much like we were [a
pawn](http://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2026/08/15/uno-nunca-se-habia-sentido-
tan-peon-de-otro-pais-pablo-mckinney-sobre-la-presion-de-eeuu-a-republica-
dominicana/) of another country.” Leaders of small left-leaning Dominican
political formations [criticized](https://listindiario.com/la-
republica/ciudad/20260813/opinan-rd-actua-presion-estados-unidos_917978.html)
their government, among them: Minou Tavárez Mirabal, founder of the Democratic
Option; Guillermo Moreno, president of the Alliance for the Country; and María
Teresa Cabrera, president of the Broad Front.

The diplomats arrived in Havana five days later. Vice-Chancellor Josefina
Vidal [commented](http://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2026/08/19/cuba-recibe-a-
los-10-diplomaticos-expulsados-de-republica-dominicana-y-denuncia-presion-de-
washington/) that, “Dominican officials were unable to offer one reason
justifying their decision, because there are none.” But serving their US
overseers would have been reason enough. The timing of the action with Fidel
Castro’s birthday would have pleased them.

At the UN General Assembly in October 2025, the DR abstained rather than vote
its customary approval of an annual resolution calling for the US blockade of
Cuba to end. In November 2025 and again six months later, Dominican
authorities opened up two of the country’s airports to the comings and goings
of US military aircraft. Prompted by the US, Dominican President Luis Abinader
[canceled](https://mst-rd.org/2026/03/08/abinader-reafirma-su-sumision-a-eeuu-
en-la-cumbre-derechista-de-trump/) the 10th Summit of the Americas which he
was to have hosted in Punto Cana in late 2025. He had previously disinvited
Cuba, Nicaragua, and Venezuela.

The DR [joined](https://www.vistazo.com/politica/nacional/quito-sera-sede-de-
la-alianza-para-desarrollo-en-democracia-DC4554656) with the right-wing
governments of Panama, Costa Rica, Ecuador to form the so-called Alliance for
Democratic Development (ADD). The group fosters commercial and political
cooperation under US tutelage. The Abinader government joined those nations in
[sending](https://www.diariolibre.com/politica/general/2025/12/18/rd-y-
aliados-add-respaldan-medidas-de-elecciones-en-honduras/3381959) electoral
observers to Honduras’s most recent presidential elections, venue for US
interference. Under US auspices, the compliant Dominican government joined 10
other rightwing regional governments in March, 2026 in Florida to form the so-
called “Shield of the Americas.” The meeting centered on building support for
US military interventions against “narcoterrorism.”

**History of domination**

US sway over the DR [has been long](https://espaillat.house.gov/media/in-the-
news/remedying-past-unlawful-military-interventions-case-dominican-republic)
in the making. The US government proposed to annex the nation during the
Ulysses Grant administration. It carried out a military occupation from 1916
until 1924. Only at its end of the brutal Rafael Trujillo dictatorship
(1930-1961) did the US back off from supporting it.

President Juan Bosch took office in 1963, four years after the victory of
Cuba’s Revolution. He introduced progressive reforms and was opposed to the DR
becoming “a base [of operations](https://miu.do/relaciones-dominico-cubanas-
mas-alla-de-un-gobernante-de-turno/) for the CIA against the Cuban
Revolution.” The result was a military coup that removed him seven months
later.

A group of young officers in April 1965 deposed the coup government. They
sought to return Juan Bosch’s to power. The US government, apprehensive about
another Caribbean revolution, carried out a military invasion. US troops by
the tens of thousands occupied the country for 11 months;
[4000](https://www.trenchart.us/p/in-1965-american-and-dominican-tanks)
Dominicans died.

This was a watershed moment. The occupation and subsequent presidency of
Joaquin Balaguer (1966-1978) introduced aggressive modes of control. Balaguer
presided over oppression of social movements and tolerated paramilitary
violence in the countryside.

The center-left governments arriving after the Balaguer era of oppression
included a repeat and tamed Balaguer presidency (1986-1996). They managed a
few democratic openings, while emphasizing neoliberal reforms. Large-scale
migration of Dominicans to the United States was “act[ing] as a [safety
valve](https://voljournals.utk.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1008&context=utk_polipubs)
alleviating pressure for change.”

**Considerations of race and social class**

The US and the DR are as one in carrying out racial oppression and beating up
on Haiti. Cooperation shows in the illegal arms and the [coup
plotters](https://www.hrw.org/report/2004/02/27/haiti-recycled-soldiers-and-
paramilitaries-march) entering Haiti from the US. The Dominican government is
building an anti-migrant wall along its Haitian border.

Anti-Black hatred has long prevailed in the DR. Haitians and their families
have lived there for generations. They are mostly undocumented and regularly
suffer abuse. As a low-paid labor force, they are essential for Dominican
agriculture. Even so, by the end of 2025 the Abinader government had forcibly
[deported](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/haitians-displaced-by-violence-
face-deportation-after-fleeing-to-dominican-republic) over 200,000 Haitians at
a rate of 10,000 deportations per week. A 2013 court
[ruling](https://www.justiceinitiative.org/publications/deportation-and-
citizenship-dominican-republic-unanswered-questions) depriving Haitians of
birthright citizenship opened the door for the deportations.

But Haitians are far from the only DR residents living difficult lives. In
fact, [14%](https://www.theglobaleconomy.com/Dominican-
Republic/poverty_ratio_high_range/) of all Dominicans lived on less than $5.50
per day in 2024. The Dominican minimum wage,
[$200-$300](https://www.compactmag.com/article/the-island-at-the-end-of-
history/) a month, is the [third
lowest](https://www.bloomberglinea.com/2024/01/02/asi-quedaron-los-salarios-
minimos-de-2024-en-latinoamerica-estos-son-los-cambios/?ref=compactmag.com) in
the Americas. Half of the DR’s population in 2024 accounted for only
[11.4%](https://wid.world/country/dominican-republic/) of the income generated
there, and only [4.6%](https://wid.world/country/dominican-republic/) of the
accumulated wealth.

There’s more to the story. The DR’s [5.1%](https://www.trade.gov/country-
commercial-guides/dominican-republic-market-overview) GDP growth in 2024
testifies to enrichment. The nation’s president is worth some [$76
million](https://www.compactmag.com/article/the-island-at-the-end-of-
history/). President Abinader formerly headed the ABICOR group of tourism-
related companies. Latin America’s
[richest](https://www.instagram.com/p/CfUSZx4LDtU/) president has soul-mates;
[16.9%](https://wid.world/country/dominican-republic/) of all the income
generated in 2024 belonged to only 1% of the population. That sector accounted
for [24.9%](https://wid.world/country/dominican-republic/) of that year’s
accumulated wealth.

Political resistance is weak. The small leftist political parties mentioned in
a recent [report](https://newpol.org/issue_post/the-dominican-left/) are more
reformist than revolutionary and are far removed from unified struggle. A few
support the neoliberal reforms being advanced by mainstream parties. The
report has it that non-involvement of youth represents the Dominican left’s
principal failing. There are “almost no leftist worker or student
organizations …[and] a draconian [labor
code](https://newpol.org/issue_post/the-dominican-left/) … prohibits strikes.”

**Cuba represents hope**

This report on the expulsion of the Cuna diplomats has covered political and
historical realities of the Dominican Republic and the government’s
subservience to US interests. Dominicans’ historic ties with Cuba are a
necessary part of the story. In that regard, the notion of hope as projected
by Cuba still prevails in the DR. Hope sparks ideas of political change, and
the US takes notice.

Miguel Mejía, general secretary of the United Left Movement, one of the
aforementioned small political parties in the DR, also denounced the expulsion
of the Cuban diplomats. He explored the history of Cuba-DR relations.

Miguel Mejía [condemns](https://miu.do/relaciones-dominico-cubanas-mas-alla-
de-un-gobernante-de-turno/) the DR government’s action as “breaking a long-
standing tradition in bilateral relations and representing an unfortunate
exception.” He cites “bonds … forged by the peoples themselves” … [resulting
from] unique events that history has brought about between our two peoples.”

He sees a “two-way channel fueled by waves of migration in both directions
[since the 19th century]” He proposes that, “This brotherhood—so deeply
rooted, so profound and robust—has never been and will never be broken
regardless of the decisions made by any ruling leader.”

Now, the “Dominican people, regardless of ideologies and political
preferences, are mobilizing against this shameful measure [of expelling the
diplomats], which does not fit within the tradition described and reveals a
very dangerous and unpopular subservience to the U.S. government.”

He is saying that people of his Caribbean nation, and by extension, peoples
elsewhere, have special regard for Cuba. They see Cuba as a forerunner of a
better political way. The example of Cuba validates their own hopes. It’s no
wonder that the US government bends all rules of decency in order both to
destroy Cuba’s Revolution and dull the vision of the down-and-out everywhere,
not least in the Dominican Republic.
